title: Implement Promise.all
description: Reimplement Promise.all from scratch — wait for every input to resolve, preserve order, reject fast on the first error. Classic async interview question.

conversation.intro: How an interview about this problem would actually play out. Each section has two parts: what you'd actually say out loud, and why that move matters. Tap a section to expand.

sections.title: 1. Restate & clarify
sections.prompt: Before touching code — pin down the contract.
sections.say:
"Let me restate: I'm reimplementing `Promise.all`. Input is an iterable of promises (or values); output is a Promise that resolves to an array of resolved values *in input order*, or rejects with the first rejection. Quick clarifying questions:"

• Should I match the spec exactly — including the empty-array behavior (resolves to `[]`) and the mixed values-and-promises case (bare values get lifted via `Promise.resolve`)?
• Iterable input, or just arrays? Real `Promise.all` accepts any iterable; arrays are the 99% case.
• Reject semantics — first rejection wins, later results ignored? (That's standard; just confirming, because `Promise.allSettled` and `Promise.any` differ.)
• Output for resolved `undefined` values — should they appear in the array, or be skipped? (Standard says they appear.)
sections.why: The empty-input question is the one to ask — most candidates forget it, and the missing case causes a forever-pending Promise (the worst kind of bug because there's no error message). Naming `allSettled` and `any` unprompted signals you know the full Promise-combinator family and aren't going to confuse the semantics. The 'resolved undefined' question seems trivial but exposes the bug where you'd track completion by checking `out[i] !== undefined` instead of using a counter.

sections.title: 2. Brute force first (out loud)
sections.prompt: Name the simplest approach before generalizing.
sections.say:
"The simplest version is `async function promiseAll(arr) { const out = []; for (const p of arr) out.push(await p); return out; }`. It works for the happy path, but it has two real problems:"

• Serial, not parallel — each `await` blocks the next iteration. If you have 3 promises each taking 100ms, this takes 300ms instead of 100.
• No fail-fast on rejection — an early rejection still waits for prior promises to settle before throwing.

"So I need to fire all promises in parallel, then synchronize on the count. That's the Promise-constructor pattern: explicit `resolve`/`reject` callbacks, attach `.then` to each input, count completions, resolve on the last one, forward the first reject."
sections.why: Showing the for-await version first is the move that proves you understand WHY the explicit Promise constructor is needed — the natural async/await translation is serial, not parallel, and concurrency is the whole point of `Promise.all`. Most candidates skip this step and reach straight for `new Promise`; naming the parallel-vs-serial distinction explicitly is the senior signal.

sections.title: 3. Spot the pattern
sections.say:
"This is a counter-based fan-in synchronization. Fire all promises immediately, then wait for the last one to settle. The pattern: wrap the whole thing in `new Promise((resolve, reject) => …)`, preallocate `out = new Array(arr.length)`, init `done = 0`. For each input, do `Promise.resolve(item).then(v => { out[i] = v; if (++done === arr.length) resolve(out); }).catch(reject)`."

"Two critical details: preallocate `out` so out-of-order resolutions land at the right index (input order, NOT settle order), and use a counter not `out.length` — a resolved `undefined` doesn't change `length`. The first `.catch(reject)` wins because Promises can only settle once; later rejections call `reject` again but it's a no-op."
sections.why: The 'preallocate so out-of-order resolutions land at the right index' framing is the load-bearing insight. Promises resolve in WALL-CLOCK order, but `Promise.all` returns results in INPUT order — preserving that ordering is what the index-based assignment buys you. Pushing in a `.then` handler would interleave by settle-time. Articulating both the order-preservation AND the 'Promises settle once' property is what proves you understand the model, not just the boilerplate.

sections.title: 4. Trace through examples
sections.prompt: Walk three input shapes to confirm the model.
sections.intro: "Let me trace three inputs — out-of-order resolves to prove the index assignment works, the empty array to defend the early-resolve, and a rejection to show fail-fast."

examples.note: Resolves arrive out of input order; output still preserves index order.
examples.trace:
init out=[empty,empty,empty], done=0
register #0 RESOLVE(1) @0ms  → handler attached
register #1 RESOLVE(2) @50ms → handler attached
register #2 RESOLVE(3) @10ms → handler attached
--- event loop ---
t=0ms  #0 settles → out[0]=1, done=1 (not last)
t=10ms #2 settles → out[2]=3, done=2 (not last)
t=50ms #1 settles → out[1]=2, done=3 === arr.length → resolve([1,2,3]) ✓

examples.note: Empty input — must resolve to [] immediately, otherwise forever-pending.
examples.trace:
init out=[] (length 0), done=0
arr.length === 0 branch: resolve(out) = resolve([])
(forEach never runs — without the early return the outer Promise would never resolve) ✓

examples.note: First rejection wins; later resolves are silently discarded.
examples.trace:
init out=[empty,empty,empty], done=0
register #0 RESOLVE(1) @0ms, #1 REJECT('boom') @5ms, #2 RESOLVE(3) @50ms
--- event loop ---
t=0ms  #0 settles → out[0]=1, done=1 (not last)
t=5ms  #1 rejects → .catch(reject) fires → outer rejects with 'boom'
t=50ms #2 settles → would call resolve(out), but outer already settled → no-op ✓

sections.why: The out-of-order trace surfaces the load-bearing index-vs-push bug — if you'd written `out.push(v)`, you'd get `[1, 3, 2]` instead of `[1, 2, 3]`. The empty-array trace defends the early-return as a correctness requirement, not a micro-optimization (without it, `done === arr.length` never fires because the forEach skips). The rejection trace proves the 'Promises settle once' property — the third resolve is harmless because the outer Promise is already settled.

sections.title: 5. Edge cases to mention
sections.prompt: What inputs would trip up a careless implementation?
sections.say:
"Edges worth flagging:"

• Empty array → resolves to `[]`. Without an early return, the `done === length` check never fires and the outer Promise hangs forever.
• All-rejected — only the FIRST rejection's reason is exposed; the others are silently discarded. Different from `Promise.allSettled`, which surfaces every outcome.
• Mixed promises and bare values — `Promise.resolve(item)` lifts plain values into thenables, so `[1, Promise.resolve(2)]` works the same as `[Promise.resolve(1), Promise.resolve(2)]`.
• Resolved `undefined` — appears as `undefined` at its index in the output. The counter (not `out.length` or a presence check) is what makes this work.
• Sync throws inside a then-callback — caught by the next `.catch` in the chain and forwarded to `reject`. No special handling needed.
• Already-rejected promises in input — `.catch(reject)` fires in the next microtask, so the outer rejects after one microtask, not synchronously. Standard for Promise behavior.
• Iterables that aren't arrays — real `Promise.all` accepts any iterable (Set, generator, etc.). The `arr.forEach` / `arr.length` version assumes array; you'd switch to `Array.from(iterable)` upfront for full spec compliance.
• Unhandled rejection if `arr` itself is `null`/`undefined` — defensive `if (!arr || typeof arr[Symbol.iterator] !== 'function')` would reject with TypeError, matching the spec.
sections.why: The empty-array and resolved-undefined edges are the two that distinguish a correct implementation from a buggy one; both are why we use the counter pattern. The iterable-vs-array distinction is the spec-completeness check — most candidates write array-only, but mentioning iterables shows you've read the spec. The `null` input edge is the defensive-coding signal: spec-compliant `Promise.all` rejects, doesn't crash.

sections.title: 6. Complexity & wrap-up
sections.prompt: How would you defend the bounds, and what does this generalize to?
sections.say:
"Time is O(n) for the setup (registering handlers on each promise), then it waits for the slowest promise — so wall-clock latency is `max(promise_durations)`, not `sum`. That's the whole win over sequential `await`.

Space is O(n) — the `out` array preallocated to input length, plus one closure per promise for the `.then` handler.

The synchronization primitive here — fire all, count completions, resolve on last or reject on first — is the foundation for the rest of the Promise-combinator family. Variations: `Promise.allSettled` waits for ALL to settle (resolves never reject, returns `{status, value/reason}` objects) — same fan-in counter, no fail-fast. `Promise.any` resolves on the first FULFILLMENT and rejects only if ALL fail (AggregateError) — invert the success/fail roles. `Promise.race` resolves or rejects on the first settle of any kind — settle-once, no counter at all. Each is a one-line change to this skeleton."
sections.why: Walking through the entire Promise-combinator family by relating each to this skeleton is the transfer move — it proves you see this as a *template* (concurrent fan-in with configurable settle rule), not a one-off implementation. The latency claim — `max` not `sum` — is the user-visible payoff and the right thing to highlight for a hiring manager who cares about real performance, not just algorithmic analysis.

walkthrough.intro: Step through promiseAll. Each input promise is described as `{resolveAfter, value}` (or `{rejectAfter, reason}`). The trace simulates resolution by sorting by `resolveAfter` and yielding one step per resolve — so you watch out-of-order resolves land at the right index, see the `done` counter climb, and see the first rejection short-circuit the rest.

examples.label: [ready→1, after 50ms→2, after 10ms→3] resolve out of order → [1,2,3] (preserved by index)
[ready→1, REJECT 'boom' after 5ms, after 50ms→3] → first reject wins

trace: yield { line: 1, label: `enter promiseAll(arr) — arr.length=${arr.length}`, state: { arr } };
yield { line: 3, label: `preallocate out=Array(${arr.length}) — slots empty so out-of-order resolves still land at the right index`, state: { arr, out: out.map(() => null), done } };
yield { line: 6, label: 'arr.length === 0 — resolve(out) immediately with []', state: { arr, out: [], done, returns: JSON.stringify([]) } };
yield { line: 7, label: 'arr.forEach((item, i) => Promise.resolve(item).then(...).catch(reject))', state: { arr, out: out.map(() => null), done } };
const desc = p.rejectAfter !== undefined ? `REJECT('${p.reason}') after ${p.rejectAfter}ms` : `RESOLVE(${JSON.stringify(p.value)}) after ${p.resolveAfter}ms`;
yield { line: 9, label: `register #${i}: Promise.resolve(arr[${i}]) → ${desc} (then/catch handlers attached)`, state: { arr, out: out.map(v => v === undefined ? null : v), done, i, desc } };
.map((p, i) => ({ i, when: p.rejectAfter !== undefined ? p.rejectAfter : p.resolveAfter, reject: p.rejectAfter !== undefined, value: p.value, reason: p.reason }))

yield { line: 10, label: `--- event loop tick: settle in time order [${order.map(o => '#' + o.i + '@' + o.when + (o.reject ? '×' : '✓')).join(', ')}] ---`, state: { arr, out: out.map(() => null), done, order } };
yield { line: 14, label: `#${ev.i} would settle but outer already rejected — ignored`, state: { arr, out: out.map(v => v === undefined ? null : v), done, settled } };

yield { line: 14, label: `#${ev.i} REJECTS with '${ev.reason}' — outer .catch(reject) fires; later results ignored`, state: { arr, out: out.map(v => v === undefined ? null : v), done, settled, returns: 'REJECTED: ' + ev.reason } };

yield { line: 11, label: `#${ev.i} resolves with ${JSON.stringify(ev.value)} — out[${ev.i}] = ${JSON.stringify(ev.value)}, done → ${done}`, state: { arr, out: out.map(v => v === undefined ? null : v), done, settled } };
yield { line: 12, label: `done (${done}) === arr.length (${arr.length}) — resolve(out) = ${JSON.stringify(out)}`, state: { arr, out: [...out], done, settled, returns: JSON.stringify(out) } };

notes: Wrap each entry with `Promise.resolve()` — values may be raw, not promises, but you still want a microtask boundary.
Track completion with a counter, not by checking `out` for empty slots. A resolved `undefined` is still a real result.
Empty input must resolve to `[]` synchronously (well, in a microtask). Forgetting this gives a forever-pending promise.

questions.q: Why preallocate `out = new Array(arr.length)` instead of pushing as each resolves?
options: `new Array(n)` allocates a contiguous buffer that the engine fills atomically — `.push` would tear under concurrent then-handlers
Promises may resolve out of order — assigning by index preserves input order
`.push` inside a `.then` callback executes on a different microtask queue than the constructor, so it skips the outer Promise's resolve
Preallocating sets `out.length` upfront, which is what makes the `done === out.length` completion check valid

questions.q: What happens when one input rejects?
options: Other inputs are cancelled via `AbortSignal` and the outer promise rejects with an AggregateError
Other inputs keep running, but the outer promise rejects with the first error and ignores later results
It waits for all to settle, then collects errors into a `.errors` array on the rejection reason
It silently resolves with `undefined` at the rejected index and keeps the other resolutions
`.then` directly on a non-thenable returns `undefined`, silently dropping the value from the output
Items may be plain values; Promise.resolve normalizes them to thenables
It defers the value to a different microtask queue so the outer Promise constructor's resolve can complete first
`Promise.resolve` triggers internal reference-counting so the runtime can GC each input once it settles
`undefined` — there are no results to package into an array
A forever-pending Promise — `done === length` is `0 === 0` which never re-fires
It should reject with a TypeError — an empty iterable is invalid input by the spec

exercises.prompt: Fill in promiseAll so [Promise.resolve(1), 2, Promise.resolve(3)] logs [1,2,3].

blanks.hint: static Promise method that wraps a value
forward errors to the outer promise

L3.prompt: Implement promiseAll(arr) that resolves to an in-order array of resolved values, or rejects with the first error. Test with a mix of promises and bare values; also test the rejection path.
hints: Wrap each entry in Promise.resolve() so plain values become thenables.
Assign results by index; track completion with a counter.
Forward the first .catch directly to the outer reject — later errors are ignored.
